n: Some people report a recent atrocity: Pilate had killed Galileans while they were offering sacrifices, mixing their blood with that of their animals. History doesn’t otherwise record this incident, but it fits Pilate’s known brutality.

f.g: Pontius Pilate, Roman governor of Judea about AD 26–36.
Killed them at the temple while they worshipped.

n: Many assumed disaster was punishment for special sin. Jesus challenges that idea: were these victims worse sinners than everyone else?
No, He says — but everyone needs to repent. Rather than speculating about others’ sins, look to your own heart.

f.g: Be destroyed — both physically and spiritually.

n: Jesus adds an accident: a tower near the Pool of Siloam collapsed, killing eighteen. Were they guiltier than everyone else in Jerusalem?

f.g: A district and pool at the southern end of Jerusalem.

n: Again, no. Tragedies don’t sort the guilty from the innocent. The real lesson: all need repentance, and life is uncertain.

f.g: Some see a foreshadowing of Jerusalem’s destruction in AD 70.

n: A parable: a vineyard owner keeps finding no fruit on his fig tree. Fig trees were sometimes planted in vineyards. Israel is often pictured as a fig tree or vine.
After three years of coming up empty, he orders it cut down — why let it drain the soil? Some see a hint of Jesus’ three years of ministry to His people.

f.g: The gardener who cares for the vines.
Uses up, takes up space uselessly.

n: The gardener pleads for one more year. He will dig around it and fertilize it. This pictures Christ’s patient intercession and extra care for us.

f.g: Fertilize it with manure.

f.w: let it alone this year also

n: If it bears fruit, good. If not, it will be cut down. Mercy is generous but not endless — there is a time to repent.

f.w: if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down

n: This is the last time Luke shows Jesus teaching in a synagogue. He uses the Sabbath to bring rest and healing.

f.g: The seventh day, Saturday — a day of rest and worship.

n: A woman has been bent double for eighteen years, unable to stand upright. Luke describes it as a spirit causing her infirmity.

f.g: A disabling condition linked to an evil influence.
Bent over.

n: Jesus notices her and calls her forward, announcing her freedom before she even asks. He sees those whom others overlook.

f.g: You are set free.

n: He lays His hands on her, and she instantly stands upright and praises God. Eighteen years of bondage end in a moment.
The synagogue ruler is indignant. Afraid to confront Jesus directly, he scolds the crowd: come to be healed on the six workdays, not on the Sabbath.

f.w: six days in which men ought to work

n: Jesus calls this hypocrisy. They untie their own animals to water them on the Sabbath. Compassion for livestock is allowed — why not for people?

f.g: Donkey.
Animal pen or manger.

n: She is a daughter of Abraham — part of God’s covenant people — and Satan has bound her for eighteen years. What day could be better for her release than the day of rest?

f.g: A rare phrase honoring her as an heir of the covenant.

n: His opponents are put to shame, while ordinary people rejoice at all the wonderful things He is doing.

f.g: Opponents.

n: Jesus asks what God’s kingdom can be compared to. He uses simple images to describe something vast.

f.g: Compare.

n: The kingdom begins as small as a mustard seed but grows into a large plant where birds nest. From a few disciples, the Church would spread across the earth.

f.g: Grew.

n: He offers a second image of the kingdom’s growth.

f.g: Compare.

n: A woman works a little yeast into a large batch of flour until the whole batch rises. The gospel works quietly from within until it transforms everything.

f.g: About 40 pounds of flour — enough bread for a large gathering.

n: Luke reminds us that Jesus is steadily traveling toward Jerusalem, teaching as He goes.
Someone asks a speculative question: will only a few be saved? Jesus turns it into a personal challenge.

f.w: are there few that be saved?

n: Instead of giving a number, He urges: make every effort to enter through the narrow door. Many will want in but won’t be able to.

f.g: Greek agōnizomai, to struggle or agonize, as an athlete competes.
Narrow door.

n: Once the owner has shut the door, those outside will knock and plead, but he will say he doesn’t know them. There comes a point when it is too late.
They protest that they ate with Him and heard Him teach in their streets. Being near Jesus is not the same as following Him.

f.w: We have eaten and drunk in thy presence

n: He repeats that He does not know them and sends them away as doers of evil. Familiarity without obedience saves no one.
They will weep in anguish when they see the patriarchs and prophets inside God’s kingdom while they themselves are cast out.

f.g: Grinding teeth — an image of bitter regret and anguish.

n: People from every direction — Gentiles from all nations — will come and sit at God’s great feast.

f.w: from the east, and from the west

n: Some who seem last now will be first, and some who seem first will be last. God’s judgments often overturn human expectations.
Some Pharisees warn Jesus to flee because Herod Antipas wants to kill Him. Whether friendly or trying to scare Him off, they urge Him to leave.

f.g: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea.

n: Jesus calls Herod a “fox” — sly and destructive. Herod cannot stop Him; He will finish His work on His own schedule and reach His goal.

f.g: In Jewish idiom a fox could suggest craftiness or insignificance.
Brought to completion — His mission fulfilled.

n: He must continue His journey, for a prophet is killed in Jerusalem, not elsewhere. His words are full of sorrowful irony.

f.w: a prophet perish out of Jerusalem
f.g: It would be unfitting for a prophet to die anywhere but Jerusalem.

n: Jesus grieves over Jerusalem. Like a mother hen sheltering her chicks, He longed to gather and protect its people, but they refused. Christ uses this same image to the Nephites.

f.w: as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings

n: Their “house” — likely the temple and city — will be left desolate. They will not see Him again until they welcome Him with the words of Psalm 118, both at His triumphal entry and ultimately at His Second Coming.

f.w: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord

f.g: Abandoned, empty.
